Invesco Real Estate launches PBSA platform for affordable student housing in Seoul
article:
Invesco Real Estate, the global real estate investment arm of Invesco Limited, has launched a purpose-built student accommodation (PBSA) platform in Seoul, South Korea.

The platform’s initial portfolio comprises five assets near Korea University, one of the largest and most prestigious institutions of higher education in the country.

The firm had acquired them through three forward-purchase transactions and two development sites, and they are expected to deliver more than 400 beds across a combined gross floor area of about 80,000 sq ft.

According to Invesco Real Estate, the accommodation offerings will primarily serve domestic Korean students, providing affordable purpose-built housing amid a limited supply of higher-priced alternatives.

“We are proud to deliver comfortable and economical living solutions for Seoul’s underserved student population,” said Jason Choi, funds management director at Invesco Real Estate.

The portfolio will be operated by Korean PBSA specialist, PCP Standard, which is backed by Silicon Valley-based Altos Ventures.

Invesco Real Estate says the partnership will combine global institutional capital with local operating expertise to deliver high-quality, affordable student housing at scale across South Korea.

Calvin Chou, head of Asia Pacific at Invesco Real Estate, said: “This platform launch aligns with Invesco Real Estate’s stated strategy to target Asia Pacific’s burgeoning living segment, a high-conviction theme with a long investment horizon.”

title: Christie's International Real Estate expands in mainland China with Shenzhen affiliate
article:
Luxury real estate brokerage firm Christie’s International Real Estate has expanded its presence in mainland China with the launch of a new affiliate in Shenzhen, Guangdong, following its entry into Shanghai in September.

The new company, Christie’s International Real Estate Shenzhen, is led by Xiaosheng Qiu as president, who has experience in the city’s luxury residential market and a social media presence across Weibo, Douyin and WeChat.

The affiliate will focus on prime residential submarkets, including Overseas Chinese Town (OCT), Shenzhen Bay, Qianhai and Futian Central District.

The team has established relationships with major developers and state-owned enterprises, and is marketing luxury residential projects priced from RMB30 million to over RMB500 million ($5.7 million to over $95.3 million), said Christie’s International Real Estate in an Oct 16 release.

These include CITIC City Development’s Xin Yue Bay, a waterfront development in Shenzhen Bay, and Raffles Residences at Shenzhen Bay 1, which overlooks Shenzhen Bay and the Hong Kong skyline.

Other projects include Blue Oasis Bay at OCT Harbor, comprising 93 lakefront villas with private yacht docks, and OCT’s Xin Xi, a completed waterfront development in Shekou.

The expansion comes amid stronger activity in Shenzhen’s luxury residential market. According to China Real Estate Information Corporation, 168 homes priced above RMB30 million were sold in 1Q2026, a 154.5% increase y-o-y.

According to Qiu, demand is increasingly concentrated on larger homes in prime locations such as Nanshan and Futian.

Branded residences are also gaining traction, reflecting demand for properties offering high-end design, amenities and services.

Shenzhen is a major technology and economic hub in China's Greater Bay Area, home to companies including Tencent, Huawei and BYD. The city will host the 2026 APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting in November.

The affiliate will leverage Qiu’s digital marketing network, which has a reach spanning millions of followers, alongside Christie’s International Real Estate’s global referral network to market luxury properties and advise clients on overseas investments.

Qiu said international education and cross-border business ties are driving interest among wealthy Chinese buyers in overseas real estate.

Helena Moyas de Forton, managing director for Europe, the Middle East and Africa, as well as Apac at Christie’s International Real Estate, said Shenzhen is an important market in the network’s regional expansion.

The Shenzhen launch follows the establishment of Christie’s International Real Estate Shanghai in September. The Shanghai agency will likewise focus on the eastern Chinese city’s prime residential submarkets, including Xintiandi and The Bund.

Christie’s International Real Estate has also established affiliates in Hong Kong, Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam, Japan, Australia and New Zealand.

title: 4 Singapore Blue-Chip Stocks I Will Buy with S$40,000
article:
Having spare cash on hand is always a great feeling.
However, leaving it in a bank account where
inflation
gradually erodes its purchasing power is rarely the best move.
Instead, deploying those funds into solid, dependable businesses allows your wealth to compound over time.
Blue-chip stocks
immediately come to mind for reliability because they possess proven track records of navigating both booming economies and market downturns.
If you have S$40,000 ready to invest, allocating S$10,000 to each of these four promising Singapore blue chips can offer a balanced blend of income and growth.
CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust
(SGX: C38U)
CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust, or CICT, is a retail and commercial
real estate investment trust
(REIT) with a resilient portfolio of properties across Singapore, Australia, and Germany.
The trust continues to demonstrate strong operating performance, delivering a 7.1% year-on-year (YoY) increase in its distribution per unit (DPU) to S$0.0602 for the first half of 2026 (1H2026).
Gross revenue rose 7.5% YoY to S$846.8 million, while net property income (NPI) expanded to S$630.5 million.
The growth came mainly from CICT taking full ownership of CapitaSpring and new income from Gallileo, partly offset by the sale of Bukit Panjang Plaza.
More growth is on the way.
CICT completed its purchase of Paragon on Orchard Road on 1 July 2026, while its sale of Asia Square Tower 2 is expected to complete in 2H2026.
Portfolio occupancy improved 0.4 percentage points quarter on quarter to 95.6%, with the retail segment holding steady at 97.7%.
Rental reversions remained positive, at 4% for its Singapore retail portfolio and 6.5% for the office portfolio.

Singapore Exchange Limited
(SGX: S68)
As the operator of Singapore’s stock exchange, Singapore Exchange Limited, or SGX, provides the essential multi-asset infrastructure for trading equities, fixed income, currencies, and derivatives.
The bourse operator reported a milestone performance for its fiscal year 2026 (FY2026), with net revenue climbing 13.9% YoY to S$1.5 billion.
Net profit rose a more modest 7.8% YoY to S$698.4 million, weighed down by a S$53.4 million goodwill impairment on Scientific Beta and weaker investment gains.
Stripping these out, adjusted net profit surged 24.6% to S$759.5 million.
On the back of these results, SGX proposed total FY2026 dividends of S$0.57 per share, up from S$0.375 a year ago.
This includes a one-off additional dividend of S$0.125, funded by gains from selling investments, and is subject to shareholder approval on 23 October 2026.
Management guided for 6% to 8% medium-term revenue growth excluding treasury income, and quarterly dividend increases of 0.25 cents through FY2028.

DBS Group Holdings Ltd
(SGX: D05)
DBS is Singapore’s largest bank by market capitalisation and offers comprehensive services ranging from consumer banking and wealth management to institutional and treasury operations.
The banking giant pulled off a sterling performance for the second quarter of 2026 (2Q2026) with total income climbing 6% YoY to S$6.1 billion, crossing the S$6 billion mark for the first time.
Net interest income slipped 2% YoY to S$3.6 billion as lower interest rates weighed on margins.
Despite its net interest margin narrowing by 18 basis points to 1.87%, 8% loan growth and stable asset quality (1.0% non-performing loan ratio) helped keep core earnings resilient.
Non-interest income surged 21% YoY to S$2.5 billion, propelled by a 42% jump in wealth management fees and a 30% rise in treasury customer sales, more than offsetting lower margins.
The board declared an interim dividend of S$0.66 per share plus a capital return dividend of S$0.15, bringing the quarterly payout to S$0.81 per share.
Management also raised its full-year guidance, expecting 2026 total income to exceed 2025 levels and commercial book non-interest income to grow in the mid-teens, led by wealth management.

Singapore Technologies Engineering Ltd
(SGX: S63)
Singapore Technologies Engineering, or STE, is a global technology and engineering group specialising in aerospace, smart city, defence, and public security solutions.
In 1H2026, the group delivered strong financial growth, with revenue rising 11.1% YoY to S$6.6 billion and net profit surging 27.1% to S$512.1 million.
Performance was buoyed by double-digit revenue gains in Commercial Aerospace and Urban Solutions.
Profit also got a lift from a 14.9% drop in net finance costs.
Free cash flow improved to S$591.6 million from S$484.6 million a year ago.
As at 30 June 2026, the group held cash and cash equivalents of S$255.3 million, down from S$576.4 million at 31 December 2025, while total borrowings eased to S$4.7 billion from S$4.8 billion over the same period.
Shareholder returns increased alongside the solid results, with total dividends for the half reaching S$0.09 per share – up from S$0.08 a year ago – and another S$0.05 payout planned for 3Q2026.
Backed by a record order book of S$35.7 billion, management remains confident in maintaining a strong growth trajectory through the rest of the year.

Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation Limited
(SGX: O39), or OCBC, has long been a staple dividend-paying

.
Someone who bought shares of the bank a decade ago would have held through various
interest rate
cycles, including low rates during the pandemic and the 2022-2023 rate surge.
What matters, however, for income investors is how much in dividends the bank has paid over the last ten years.
So let’s put S$20,000 into OCBC in October 2016, count each dividend, and see how the starting yield, dividend growth and the rising share price have added to the result.
How We Calculate the 10-Year OCBC Investment
The purchase price is OCBC’s closing price of S$8.69 on 10 October 2016; S$20,000 gets you 2,300 shares.
Remember, until recently, you could only purchase shares in board lot sizes of 100 shares.
Dividend per share, collected as cash, ran at S$6.328 across the ten years (S$0.32 of this was special dividends).
Excluding brokerage costs and transaction fees, and given that OCBC’s dividends are tax-exempt, you would have pocketed a sum of S$14,554.4.
What Was OCBC’s Dividend Like 10 Years Ago?
Back in 2016, OCBC paid a final dividend of S$0.36 per share, yielding roughly 4.1% given a purchase price of S$8.69.
Today’s annualised yield is lower at 3.2%, because the share price has risen faster than the dividend.
The dividend growth path wasn’t straight, though.
OCBC’s ordinary dividend climbed from S$0.37 per share in 2017 to S$0.53 by 2019, then fell to S$0.318 in 2020 as the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) asked banks to cap their 2020 dividends at 60% of 2019’s level.
OCBC then raised its ordinary dividend back to S$0.53 per share in 2021 and continued raising it to S$0.85 per share by 2024 before lowering it slightly to S$0.83 per share in 2025, likely because of lower interest rates.
The latest interim dividend for 2026 came in at S$0.47 per share, up 15% compared to a year earlier.
The starting yield tells only part of the story, because dividend growth did most of the work.

What Would the Investment Be Worth Today?
At a share price of S$29 right now, 2300 shares of OCBC are worth S$66,700.
Add S$14,554.4 in dividends, and the total stands at S$81,254.4.
This brings the total return against the initial S$20,000 investment to 306%, which works out to roughly a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 15%, with dividends taken as cash.
OCBC’s share price appreciation supplied 76% of the total return and dividends 24%; this is the perfect example of both dividend income and capital appreciation working in tandem to generate a solid total return.
What If You Reinvested Every Dividend
?
This is an illustration.
Assume each dividend bought whole shares on its payment date, at a price on a smooth path from S$8.69 to S$29, with leftover cash carried forward and no fees.
The 2,300 shares would grow to about 3,288 shares, which would be worth around S$95,000 with leftover cash.
This is a 377% return, or a 16.9% CAGR.
Much of OCBC’s price gain came recently, so earlier purchases were probably cheaper than the smooth path assumes, which makes this a conservative estimate.
Reinvesting added more than S$10,000 compared to taking the dividend as cash, significantly boosting the effect of compounding.
Your Yield on Cost Would Look Very Different
Yield on cost is the current annual dividend divided by what you paid.
On 2,300 shares, that is S$2,277, an 11.4% yield on your initial capital outlay.
A new buyer at S$29 earns 3.4%.
The same capital paid S$851 in its first year and now pays nearly three times that, given specials and dividend growth.
What Drove OCBC’s Dividend Growth?
OCBC earned S$3.5 billion in net profit in 2016 and S$7.4 billion in 2025, about 8.8% a year.
Topline grew more slowly, from S$8.5 billion to S$14.6 billion, so OCBC kept more of each dollar of revenue as profit.
Earnings per share (EPS) doubled to S$1.63.
The first half of 2026 brought another record, with profit of S$4.2 billion, up 13%.
Return on equity (ROE) went from 9.1% to 14.4% annualised.
Net interest margin (NIM) thinned to 1.73%, but wealth, fee and insurance income have made up for the lower net interest income (NII).
Capital strength kept pace with the payout.
The Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratio is still healthy at 14.0%, and OCBC targets about 50% of profit as ordinary dividends, plus 10% as a special dividend under its S$2.5 billion capital return plan (to be completed by 2026).
Acquisitions helped too: Barclays’ Singapore and Hong Kong wealth business in 2016 helped; HSBC’s Indonesian wealth business, slated for completion in 2027, could add to this.
Moving forward, sustained earnings growth is critical for the bank to maintain its dividend growth.

Could OCBC Deliver Similar Dividend Income Over the Next 10 Years?
Not by simple repetition.
OCBC currently trades at a premium earnings and book multiple of 16.7x and 2.1x, respectively, while the current starting yield is lower as well.
Lower rates have squeezed its NIM, though loan growth guidance is still healthy in the high single digits.
The non-performing loan (NPL) ratio is a clean 0.9%, but its exposure to Greater China real estate remains a risk.
The capital return plan ends in 2026, so the special dividend shouldn’t be assumed to continue indefinitely.
The HSBC Indonesia deal will also require capital.
A ten-year record is evidence about the business, not a promise of another decade of rising payout.

title: The RTS Link Countdown: Is Frasers Centrepoint Trust Built to Withstand the S$290m Retail Drain?
article:
The Singapore-Johor Bahru (JB) Rapid Transit System (RTS) Link is almost here.
The cross-border rail line is set to open in early 2027, and suburban mall owners have reason to pay attention.
A study commissioned by the Singapore Business Federation, the Restaurant Association of Singapore and the Singapore Retailers Association expects Singapore residents to spend S$1.05 billion more in JB each year once the RTS opens.
JB visitors, for their part, are expected to spend S$756 million more in Singapore.
Net it out, and around S$290 million a year flows out of Singapore.
That’s roughly 0.4% of the country’s 2025 retail and food-and-beverage (F&B) sales.
For a
suburban mall landlord
like
Frasers Centrepoint Trust
(SGX: J69U), or FCT, that’s an impact worth watching.
Which of FCT’s malls sit in the firing line?
Here’s the thing: the outflow will be uneven.
The west faces the largest net outflow at S$104 million.
The north-east is a close second at S$103 million.
The north comes in at S$82 million, and the east at just S$25 million.
FCT’s malls in the north and north-east could feel the impact.
Causeway Point and Northpoint City sit in the north and make up a little over 40% of FCT’s portfolio valuation.
NEX, Hougang Mall and Waterway Point sit in the north-east, the region facing the second-largest outflow.
How did FCT fare in its latest half-year?
Gross revenue and net property income (NPI) each rose by more than 20% year on year in the first half of the fiscal year ending 30 September 2026 (1H FY2026).
However,
distribution per unit
(DPU) grew just 1.4%.

Much of the gap comes down to a larger unit count.
FCT paid for its Northpoint City South Wing acquisition, completed in May 2025, partly by issuing new units.
The weighted average unit count rose from around 1.82 billion to about 2.04 billion.
More units mean income gets spread more thinly.
Are FCT’s tenants feeling the strain already?
In 3Q FY2026, shopper traffic rose 2.4% year on year.
Tenant sales grew just 0.2%, down from 4.4% growth a year ago.
The manager put this down to tenancy churn.
FCT signed 69 new-to-portfolio tenancies in the first nine months of FY2026, up from 59 a year earlier. New tenants need time to fit out their stores and win over regulars.
The refresh may be necessary with the RTS on the horizon.
How is FCT refreshing its north-east malls?
Both of FCT’s asset enhancement initiatives (AEIs) are in the north-east.
At Hougang Mall, over 98% of the AEI space is committed, and more than 40% of the incoming tenants are new to the mall.
Over at NEX, Phase 1 of the AEI at the former Isetan space has secured 87% pre-commitment, and 73% of the committed tenants are new-to-mall brands.
FCT holds a 50% effective interest in NEX.
Causeway Point could be next.
Metro has signalled it will close its department store there when the lease expires.
The change looks overdue.
Metro takes up 3% of FCT’s retail net lettable area (NLA) but contributes just 1.6% of gross rental income.
We could see FCT carve up the space for several tenants.
Where does FCT’s next leg of growth come from?
FCT plans to sell White Sands for S$467 million, an 8.4% premium to valuation.
Net proceeds of S$454.1 million will repay debt, and gearing should fall from 40% to 36.5%.
The trade-off is a 1.9% pro-forma dip in DPU.
FCT is giving up some rental income for more room to borrow.
Some of that room will go to Bayshore Drive.
FCT will take half of the commercial component, which carries a total development cost of around S$613 million at a 5% yield on cost.
The site connects directly to Bedok South MRT station, and 10,000 new homes are coming to the area.
This is new territory.
Until now, FCT has grown by buying and enhancing malls, not building them.
The capital won’t earn a return until FY2031, so patience is key.
Keep an eye on
interest costs
too.
Fixed-rate debt fell to 65.7% of borrowings in 3Q FY2026 from 76.2% a year ago.
With more floating-rate debt on the books, a rise in rates would now hit DPU harder.

Track tenant sales against traffic at FCT’s north and north-east malls over the quarters that follow.
If shoppers keep coming but spend less, the drain is biting.
If tenant sales pick up as the new tenants settle in, the refresh is doing its job.
Then ask yourself one last question.
Is that recovery showing up in DPU, or only in headline revenue?
The answer could define FCT’s long-term future.

title: Toyota to debut its own version of Tesla EV-making tech in China
article:
(Oct 16): Toyota Motor Corp plans to use its own gigacasting machinery to make electric vehicles at a US$2 billion Lexus factory in China, part of its push to reverse a sales decline in the world’s biggest car market.

The Japanese manufacturer is developing the technology for the site “in-house,” said chief technology officer Hiroki Nakajima, when asked if Toyota is procuring gigacasting machines from a local supplier. The Shanghai plant is under construction and due to start producing cars in 2027.

“This is a big chance to change the manufacturing system,” Nakajima said during an interview in Brussels. “Every time, the starting point is in house.”

The Lexus site will mark Toyota’s first use of the giant presses, part of an effort to become competitive in China, where local brands are dominating on EVs. Pioneered by Tesla Inc and used by the likes of BYD Co and Xiaomi Corp, gigacast presses can mould entire chassis sections in one piece, replacing dozens of parts that previously needed to be welded together. The process helps manufacturers save on time, equipment, labour and cost.

Toyota is currently conducting trials of the technology in Japan, the company said. It declined to comment on potential suppliers related to its gigacasting efforts.

The downside is that the technology is expensive and offers less flexibility when producing different models. Accidents tend to be more costly as replacement parts are bigger.

See also: Toku lifts revenue growth guidance; expects growth for FY2026 to exceed 20%

Carmakers often work closely with die-casting suppliers such as Italy’s Idra Group or China’s Haitian to tailor the machines to their needs.

Toyota and its European peers have been contending with a shrinking market in China, where consumers are shying away from expensive purchases due to an ongoing real estate crisis. They’re also heavily favouring EVs from local brands. Toyota’s sales in China are down 19% after the first eight months of the year.

Nakajima was speaking at Toyota’s technical centre in Brussels, showing off the latest technologies the company is working on. These include advancements in hybrid engines, EVs and hydrogen fuel cells, as Toyota continues with its multi-pathway strategy pushing all powertrains.

See also: TSMC’s profit surpasses expectations after AI orders rush in

A major effort is being made on automation in factories to speed up development times, with Toyota spending billions of dollars on the latest equipment.

title: UK said to raise taxes on banks in budget this month
article:
(Oct 16): UK Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey is set to raise taxes on banks to fund cost-of-living support for voters and stabilise the public finances, as he looks for sources of revenue that won’t violate Labour Party campaign pledges.

An increase in bank taxes is one of the major measures that Healey submitted to the Office for Budget Responsibility ahead of his first fiscal event on Oct 28, according to people familiar with the matter. The move will likely involve increasing the bank surcharge that’s levied on top of the standard corporation tax rate, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss plans that had not been announced.

The proposal to increase the 3% bank surcharge was reported by the Guardian newspaper earlier on Thursday. The rate was set at 8% until 2023, when Healey’s Conservative predecessor, Jeremy Hunt, reduced it. Fully reversing it would raise £2 billion (US$2.7 billion or $3.4 billion).

A Treasury spokesperson declined to comment on the plans. “As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumours, speculation or proposals,” the Treasury said.

Shares in NatWest Group plc and Lloyds Banking Group plc fell more than 2% in early trading on Friday, making them the worst performers in the FTSE 100 index. Barclays plc and HSBC Holdings plc, which have more international business, were less affected by the news.

Speculation about bank taxes has swirled since Prime Minister Andy Burnham took power in July, and Healey declined to rule out the move while attending International Monetary Fund (IMF) meetings in Bangkok this week. That’s despite describing the City of London’s finance industry as “part of the jewel” in the British economic crown during an interview with Bloomberg in the Thai capital.

See also: Airtel Money shares slip in debut after biggest London IPO in five years

“My observations on the banks are just that people too often see them as big distant financial institutions, when they are hardwired into the economic fabric,” Healey subsequently told reporters when pressed on whether he favoured an increase in bank taxes. “That said, I have got decisions to take in the budget, and I will set those out in two weeks’ time.”

Burnham has promised to deliver “breathing space” for Britons facing sharp increases in energy bills and mortgage costs in the wake of the US-led war against Iran. Healey confirmed at the IMF meetings that any such support would be temporary and targeted to the neediest.

Options the Treasury has been drawing up for the budget include spending more on the warm homes discount — currently a £150 discount on energy bills for people on low income or receiving certain welfare payments — and freezing fuel duty.

See also: Revolut’s Storonsky says he’s coming for JPMorgan’s US crown

Healey is also seeking to repair the public finances, after a rise in borrowing costs linked to the war is estimated to have halved the £23.6 billion fiscal buffer he inherited from former chancellor Rachel Reeves. He also needs to close a gap in defence spending.

Healey’s move towards taxing banks follows an intense lobbying campaign from left-wing think tanks and trade unions. They have been urging the Treasury to target the industry after it enjoyed recent windfall profits, spurred by higher interest rates.

In August, HSBC Holdings plc reported a second-quarter profit increase of 60% to US$10.1 billion. The rest of the big four, including Barclays plc, Natwest Group plc and Lloyds Banking Group plc, posted cumulative profits in the first-half of almost £30 billion.

The bank surcharge was reduced to 3% from 8% in 2023 to offset some of the increase in corporation tax that year to 25% from 19%. That left UK banks paying 28% rather than 33%, which would have made them more highly taxed them elsewhere.

But those sceptical about proposals to raise bank taxes include Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey, who has previously warned that raising costs on the firms would result in higher mortgage rates and risk undermining financial stability.

Asked about the proposal at an Institute of International Finance meeting in Bangkok, Bailey declined to comment. “It’s not for me. I am not involved. It’s for the Treasury,” he said.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

UK Finance, which represents British banks, said the sector already makes a major contribution to the public finances and faces materially higher tax rates in London than other financial centers. “Further tax increases would weaken the UK’s competitiveness, discourage investment and job creation, and work against the government’s ambition to deliver growth in every postcode,” the group said.

Healey has insisted that he will maintain fiscal discipline at his budget, stressing that he will continue to meet the UK’s main budgetary rules, which require day-to-day spending to be covered by tax receipts by 2029/30, and for debt to be falling as a share of the economy.

Healey met with the heads of Britain’s big banks earlier this month and told them the UK faces a tough fiscal position, but said he hadn’t decided on whether to hike taxes on the sector. Attendees at the meeting included HSBC’s Georges Elhedery, CS Venkatakrishnan at Barclays, Charlie Nunn from Lloyds and Paul Thwaite at NatWest.

City of London executives have been fearing that Healey will impose a windfall tax on the profits of domestic banks and exempt the UK operations of international lenders in order to limit the hit to Britain’s global competitiveness, Bloomberg has previously reported.

There have been concerns among bankers that the government believes UK lenders haven’t done enough to support small businesses, and some of the revenues raised from banks could be used to lessen costs for those firms, according to people familiar with the matter.

A windfall tax on UK profits of its big four lenders could raise as much as £18.9 billion, according to a calculation from Positive Money, a group that campaigns against inequality. The Green Party has called for a 38% windfall tax on banks in order to fund a tax cut for small- and medium-sized enterprises.

The Institute for Public Policy Research, a left-leaning think tank that’s close to the Labour government, last year suggested a tax on banks to recover what it called a “staggering” state subsidy they had received as a result of the Bank of England’s quantitative easing programme.

title: Partners Group said to cut jobs in private equity unit — Bloomberg
article:
(Oct 16): Partners Group Holding AG has cut or reassigned dozens of positions in its private equity unit, as the firm seeks to boost performance under investor scrutiny.

Some of the affected staff in the division, which is run by Wolf-Henning Scheider, have exited the firm, people familiar with the matter said, while others have been moved to other parts of the company including Infrastructure and Royalties. The cuts were global and went across the hierarchy in the unit, which has over 200 staff, said the people, who asked not to be named discussing confidential information.

Partners Group has seen performance at its older portfolios trail those of some peers, which has helped fuel a surge in investor requests to return cash from its “evergreen” products. One of Europe’s largest private markets firms with US$186 billion under management, Partners is seeking to emerge from a turbulent period in which it has been targeted by a short seller firm amid doubts over its valuations.

“Partners Group’s private equity team size remains consistent with its long-term average, while we have significantly strengthened our senior operational capabilities over the past year,” the company said in a statement. “This reflects a buyout environment in which creating long-term value and driving distributions require greater operational intensity.”

The exits from the private equity team happened after one of the firm’s regular performance review exercises, a spokesman said.

Senior hires over the last year have included Tarak Mehta, Nicholas Smith Wang, Jennifer Hoh and Pete Zippelius, the spokesman added.

Partners Group shares are down about 40% this year, making the Zug-based company one of the worst-performing financial stocks in Europe at a time of sustained pressure on private equity firms generally. A recent management reshuffle, in which David Layton moved from the chief executive officer position to be chief investment officer, has done little to arrest the slide.

The company’s shares were up 0.6% at 9.20am in Zurich.

See also: CLI's 1HFY2026 operating patmi and patmi results above expectations

Partners Group has recently experienced a number of write-downs at investments, some of which were made at the peak of the post-Covid market. Private equity performance is heavily influenced by the timing of deals, with investments made at the end of the low-interest rate-era when valuations soared now often under pressure of much higher rates.

Partners Group earlier this year wrote off its investment in healthcare firm Pharmathen and is discussing handing over the keys of German toy company Schleich to its creditors. It has also been weighing injecting fresh funds into French real estate services provider Emeria SASU.

One of the firm’s flagship investments, watchmaker Breitling, has also been cutting jobs as the Swiss firm grapples with softening luxury demand and higher costs.

Like other private equity firms, Partners has struggled to offload their assets as quickly as they used to, leaving their investors waiting longer to be repaid. That has prompted some investors, in particular wealthy individuals, to seek the periodic redemptions which the evergreen structure pioneered by Partners Group allows.

At the same time, some of Partners’ more recent private equity investments have recorded stronger earnings growth than the firm has seen in its 30-year history. And in infrastructure, the firm’s newer evergreens have outperformed many large rivals, according to a recent Goldman Sachs Group Inc research report.

Partners has reacted to the redemption pressure by presenting a plan for one of its flagship private equity funds, the €6.6 billion Global Value SICAV, proposing to divide it into two sub-portfolios. Older assets are to be moved into one pocket and a smaller number of newer investments which are more likely to generate higher returns into another.

The move is aimed at giving investors who are keen on cashing out a way to do so, while letting those committed for the long-term stay invested in the fund’s more promising bets.

title: China moves to prop up stock market with selling curbs, buybacks — Bloomberg
article:
(Oct 16): China moved to stabilise its equity market by urging companies and state funds to buy shares while guiding some investors to curb selling, people familiar with the matter said.

Financial regulators held a meeting Thursday to discuss stabilisation measures for the stock market, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing private deliberations.

Authorities also issued window guidance to several major insurers, instructing them to report equity holdings, refrain from locking in losses on underwater positions, and align investment decisions with broader economic goals, according to people familiar with the matter. Meanwhile, regulators are calling on the so-called national team to accelerate stock purchases, the people said.

The coordinated interventions reflect mounting concern in Beijing over market fragility and an urgent push to prevent selling pressure from cascading into a downward spiral. Earlier this month, the securities regulator committed to bolster market-stabilisation mechanisms, expand channels for long-term institutional capital, encourage higher corporate payouts and buybacks, and ready additional policy tools.

The benchmark index is down about 10% this year and on Thursday closed at the lowest since August 2025. The decline was even more pronounced in growth-oriented shares, with the tech-heavy ChiNext Index sliding 2.9% on Thursday.

See also: China’s plan to make yuan a global currency enters faster phase

The sell-off has been concentrated in technology and AI-related shares, which had powered much of the market’s earlier gains. Chinese stocks have also been caught in a broader global technology rout, with South Korea’s Kospi plunging more than 7% on Thursday and Japan’s Nikkei 225 falling almost 5% as investors reassessed AI valuations and the outlook for interest rates.

China is facing significant economic headwinds. The economy slowed more than expected in the second quarter to the weakest in more than three years, raising pressure on policymakers to speed up public spending to ensure their annual growth goal is met.

See also: CIIE: China’s window to the world’s latest offerings

The country is due to release third-quarter GDP data next Monday. Weak consumer demand, sluggish private investment and a prolonged property downturn continue to weigh on growth.

Chinese government bonds have extended their rally this year amid a persistently weak outlook for the economy, with the 10-year benchmark yield hovering near the lowest in more than a year. The yuan has gained more than 4% against the dollar year to date, outperforming its Asian peers thanks to China’s resilient export sector.

title: Toku lifts revenue growth guidance; expects growth for FY2026 to exceed 20%

Cloud communications and AI-powered customer experience platform Toku (SGX:TKU ) says it is revising its revenue guidance for FY2026 after completing a review of its performance at the end of 3QFY2026 ended Sept 30.

title: China’s plan to make yuan a global currency enters faster phase
article:
(Oct 16): China’s campaign to promote the global use of the yuan appears to be accelerating as the authorities seek to build a more comprehensive financial ecosystem for the currency beyond just trade settlement.

Beijing is focused on developing the infrastructure needed to expand the yuan’s use in global financing and investment, and to strengthen its role as a reserve currency. This includes broadening the range of available investment products and financial instruments, such as derivatives and hedging tools, while making it easier for borrowers to issue so-called dim sum and panda bonds.

China’s challenge is no longer simply to persuade its trading partners to settle transactions in yuan. It must also ensure that the currency has sufficient liquidity, financing channels, investment products, and reserve assets to play a larger role in global portfolios and capital flows.

Here are four areas where Beijing is making progress towards the yuan’s internationalisation:

Measures to broaden offshore yuan-denominated investment products include plans to increase the scale and frequency of government bond issuance in Hong Kong, where policymakers are seeking to develop a yield curve for the currency.

See also: CIIE: China’s window to the world’s latest offerings

Hong Kong authorities are also studying the introduction of short-term yuan debt instruments and plan to launch a redesigned yuan-denominated gold futures contract.

“The next policy focus will likely be on speeding up the development of renminbi asset markets,” said Tommy Wu, a senior economist for Greater China and North Asia at Standard Chartered plc in Hong Kong. “One of the key challenges is how to capitalise on global investors’ increasing needs for diversification and attract them to increase their investment in renminbi assets.”

See also: China’s trade surplus nears US$1 tril again with export surge

Many overseas investors will be reluctant to increase their yuan holdings unless they have ways to manage volatility, interest-rate and currency risks.

China’s authorities are seeking to address these concerns in several ways, including by expanding a major derivatives trading link with Hong Kong to give foreign investors access to more onshore interest-rate products. In August, they also introduced a new set of government bond futures in Hong Kong, giving global investors another hedging tool.

“Institutions will not hold substantial renminbi balances without instruments offering suitable duration, liquidity and risk management,” said Tommy Xie, the head of Asia macro research at Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp (OCBC) in Singapore. “The missing piece is therefore not just ‘more renminbi assets’ but a full asset-liability and hedging chain.”

Mainland China and Hong Kong are both seeking to make the currency a more widely used financing vehicle by expanding onshore and offshore funding channels. China plans to make panda bond issuance and trading more accessible to overseas borrowers. Panda bonds are yuan-denominated debt issued in mainland China by foreign entities.

Hong Kong is seeking to encourage further issuance of yuan-denominated debt in the city and aims to develop an “enhanced tenor structure” for dim sum bond issuance. Dim sum bonds are securities denominated in yuan and issued outside mainland China. The city is also seeking to increase yuan liquidity, making it easier for governments and companies to raise funds in the currency.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

China’s cross-border yuan payment and settlement system is gaining traction. The annual transaction value in 2025 had almost quadrupled in 10 years to 180.2 trillion yuan (US$26.9 trillion or $34.5 trillion), based on data compiled by Bloomberg.

The expanding Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS) allows companies and financial institutions to transact more easily in yuan outside China, Standard Chartered’s Wu said.

“We could see efforts to further expand the CIPS’ usage for cross-border clearing and settlement, as well as the promotion of cross-border QR code payments, especially with Asean countries,” he said.

title: Sumitomo Life CEO targets acquisitions in Southeast Asia, US
article:
(Oct 16): Sumitomo Life Insurance Co is considering buying companies in Southeast Asia and the US as the Japanese insurer seeks to expand and diversify its income, its top executive said.

“In Japan, the population is shrinking and it’s quite difficult to assume we can capture the growth there,” President Yukinori Takada said in an interview in Singapore. “We believe in diversifying and investing in growth engines.”

Sumitomo Life and its Japanese peers are expanding overseas to counter the demographic pressures at home. Meiji Yasuda Life Insurance Co completed a US$2.3 billion (RM9.4 billion) acquisition of Legal & General America Inc earlier this year, while Nippon Life Insurance Co bought Resolution Life Group Holdings Ltd and consolidated its Australian insurance operations last year.

Takada said the company has set aside as much as one trillion yen (RM25.7 billion) for investment under its mid-term plan that runs through March 2029. It will tap overseas units Singapore Life Holdings Pte and US-based Symetra Financial Corp to look for acquisition targets in Southeast Asia and the US.

“These two regions and these two vehicles are very important to us,” he said, speaking through a translator.

Within Southeast Asia, Takada said Sumitomo Life already has minority interests in Indonesia and Vietnam and would like to expand further in Singapore as well as countries such as Thailand, Malaysia and the Philippines.

See also: IHH said to join race for TPG’s Malaysian hospitals

“The Singapore market still has potential to grow,” Takada said, adding that Income Insurance Ltd is one of the targets the Japanese insurer is considering. The goal is for Singlife to be among the top three life insurers in Singapore, according to Takada.

In the US, Sumitomo Life would prefer companies that can complement Symetra’s business rather than cannibalise it, he said.

When asked about the firm’s appetite in India, where several Japanese companies are expanding, Takada said Sumitomo Life is studying the market, though is mindful about the regulatory and cultural hurdles there.

See also: Jardine Matheson raises underlying earnings guidance for FY2026; assumes full control of Gammon Construction

Takada said he doesn’t believe in over-aggressively growing abroad. He will look for targets that are sustainable and can provide synergies to its existing businesses.

Sumitomo Life completed the acquisition of Singlife in 2024 for S$4.6 billion (RM14.6 billion) after getting approval from regulators in the city-state and Japan. It bought Symetra in 2016 for US$3.8 billion and delisted the company from the New York stock exchange after that.

Separately, Sumitomo Life sees the Bank of Japan raising interest rates two more times in the coming months, in December and April next year, according to Takada. Even as Japan’s long-term rates have risen to their highest levels in about 30 years, Takada said the firm has no intention to increase its domestic bond holdings beyond what is necessary for asset-liability management.

The insurer is investing in private credit as a diversification move to ensure portfolio stability, and doesn’t see a bubble in artificial intelligence investments, Takada said.

Founded in 1907 and based in Osaka, Sumitomo Life had assets totalling US$322.6 billion as of March 31, according to its latest annual report.

title: BOE’s Bailey sees little evidence of second-round inflation
article:
(Oct 16): Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey said there is little evidence yet of inflation becoming embedded in UK price and wage-setting.

The central bank is watching closely for signs that companies and workers are pushing up prices and wages to cover their own rising costs, setting off a second round of the inflation shock, Bailey said on Friday at the Institute of International Finance annual meeting in Bangkok.

“To the extent we have seen evidence, it’s quite subdued,” the governor said. “It’s too early.”

Inflation is above the BOE’s 2% target at 3.1% and forecast to rise to 4% in the coming months, a level that the bank itself says should provoke a policy response.

Bailey and his colleagues on the Monetary Policy Committee make their next interest-rate decision on Nov 5, when the markets expect a quarter-point hike to bring the benchmark to 4%.

The committee is increasingly split over policy and its last vote in September was tight, with a 6-3 vote in favour of holding rates.

See also: EU set to bolster its power to block Chinese imports in trade fight

Two of Bailey’s committee colleagues — external member Megan Greene and chief economist Huw Pill — have warned at other events in Bangkok against waiting for more inflation evidence. Both have been voting for rate increases, citing concern about the potential for second-round effects and the need to move fast.

Bailey has argued that policy is restrictive because the BOE was going to cut rates this year before the Iran conflict began in February. At that point, “the market was pricing a couple of cuts, and I thought that was probably pretty reasonable,” he said on Friday at the IIF event.

He was speaking after the International Monetary Fund raised its growth forecast for the UK to 1.3% this year from 1% and official UK GDP data this week showed the economy is expanding faster than expected. GDP rose 0.7% in the three months to August.

See also: ECB in no rush to act amid opposing economic forces, Kazaks says

The UK economy is proving to be “more resilient than we expected it to be,” Bailey said.

title: EU set to bolster its power to block Chinese imports in trade fight
article:
(Oct 16): The European Union (EU) is preparing to create new trade powers that could completely shut off access to its single market as part of a dramatic new push to cut the trade deficit with China.

EU leaders meeting in Brussels on Thursday asked the European Commission, which handles trade matters for the bloc, to develop a proposal by the end of the year, according to people familiar with the matter. The powers would be deployed in an extreme case where a rival, such as China, was seen as attacking the EU’s economy.

“If China engages in certain unfair trade practices, we could restrict the entry of Chinese products into the European market, including a complete closure of our market,” Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda told reporters on the sidelines of the summit. “That would be an extreme measure, a drastic instrument.”

As part of a rapidly expanding arsenal of trade powers, the commission has also begun evaluating trade data as a first step towards replicating a cap on hybrid car imports in other sectors where shipments from China — or other countries — may be surging, said a separate person, who spoke on the condition of anonymity. The commission is assessing industries including chemicals and machinery as potentially in need of safeguard measures.

European chemicals stocks got a boost, with BASF SE rising as much as 0.8% after the news, Arkema SA gaining as much as 1.2% and Lanxess AG climbing as much as 1.8%.

See also: ECB in no rush to act amid opposing economic forces, Kazaks says

A spokesperson for the commission didn’t respond to a request for comments.

The EU’s aggressive change in stance reflects increasing alarm, particularly in its German manufacturing powerhouse, over the pace at which Chinese rivals are increasing their share of markets all around the world. EU officials are trying to calibrate their policy response to stop China from flooding the continent with low-cost goods, but without triggering a trade war.

China has said it would retaliate if the EU introduces new trade tools or discriminatory restrictions targeting Chinese companies or products beyond the cap on hybrid vehicles that was agreed during talks in Beijing last week.

See also: IMF sees Asia’s growth slowing despite AI-fuelled resilience

Germany has traditionally been much more cautious about imposing any protectionist measures on China because its export-driven economy has deep commercial ties with Beijing. But German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has been persuaded that a radical change in strategy is called for after industry lobby groups appealed to the government for help.

“We will no longer stand idly by while other countries harm our economy through high subsidies, artificially devalued currencies, overcapacity and aggressive pricing,” Merz said in a speech to the German Parliament on Wednesday. “Anyone who seeks a trade conflict with us will find that we are now fighting back, with appropriate responses.”

The instrument that could be used to shut off access to the EU’s single market is seen as a so-called second-strike measure, the people familiar with the plans said. Its existence is intended to deter rivals from using unfair policies to weaken European companies or from starting a trade war against the EU with retaliatory measures.

As part of the effort to reset their trading relationship with the world’s second-biggest economy, the bloc’s executive arm is due to present additional proposals ahead of a leaders’ summit in mid-December. That package should also include new powers to incentivise European companies to diversify the range of suppliers they rely on and others to address overcapacity in China.

The EU’s trade deficit with China reached a record US$34.8 billion ($44.6 billion) in September and total Chinese exports surged 36% from a year earlier, according to China’s General Administration of Customs. China’s annual trade surplus this year is on track to exceed the US$1.2 trillion record set in 2025.

Any additional caps on EU imports will likely be based on the understanding that EU officials reached with China to limit imports of hybrid vehicles to 350,000 a year, according to the person. That means the EU will try to find a quota that is low enough to offer protection to its companies, and high enough to persuade Beijing not to retaliate.

Some countries, including Germany, are pressing the EU to quickly impose additional quotas on other types of imports to begin reducing the bloc’s massive trade deficit with China, Bloomberg reported earlier. Berlin is seeking proposals from the commission by the end of the year.

The commission doesn’t have a time frame for the new safeguard assessments, and is focusing on implementing the measures on hybrid vehicles, said the person. That agreement with China would also see Beijing cut tariffs on some EU exports of auto parts, olive oil and ice cream.

The EU is also seeking to improve market access in China and ease export procedures for critical minerals and permanent magnets.

The EU’s trade chief, Maros Sefcovic, is due to take stock of progress and discuss next steps with his Chinese counterparts early next year.

title: Asian stocks advance as chip sell-off eases
article:
(Oct 16): Asian equities rose on Friday morning, tracking gains on Wall Street as dip buyers stepped in following a chip-stock sell-off fuelled by concerns about the artificial intelligence (AI) trade.

The MSCI Asia-Pacific Index advanced 0.6%, led by stocks in South Korea. Chip stocks rose with Samsung Electronics Co and SK Hynix Inc both edging higher. Earlier, the S&P 500 erased losses and edged up to close 0.3% higher on Thursday.

A tone of caution prevailed as contracts for US benchmarks edged lower in early Asian trading. Futures for the Nasdaq 100 Index fell 0.5%. On Thursday, American depositary receipts of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) fell 1.8% after its upbeat outlook failed to quash AI buildout concerns.

Treasuries rallied on haven demand driven by this week’s sharp swings in global stocks and credit markets. The yield on the benchmark 10-year fell 13 basis points to 5.06% in the New York session. Treasury futures edged higher on Friday with US Federal Reserve (Fed) chairman Kevin Warsh set to speak in a fireside chat with International Monetary Fund managing director Kristalina Georgieva in Bangkok.

Indonesian stocks will be in focus after the country faced a potential ejection from global stock indices. Traders will also monitor Chinese markets with the European Union preparing to create new trade powers that could completely shut off access to its single market as part of a dramatic new push to cut the trade deficit with China.

See also: Stock sell-off extends to Asia as chip rout deepens

Attention now turns to whether the rebound in equities can broaden after the sell-off exposed growing unease over the heavy concentration of gains in AI-linked stocks. Signs of a rotation into other parts of the market may offer equities a firmer footing after months in which technology shares dominated returns.

“After a strong run in AI stocks the past few months, value shares got way too cheap, while tech got quite expensive amid the AI frenzy,” said Brian Frank, the president and a portfolio manager at Frank Funds. “We are still looking for companies that have good credit and trade at discounts in case growth or consumer spending ebbs on sticky inflation.”

There were already signs of a broader shift on Wall Street. An equal-weighted version of the S&P 500 Index climbed 1.4%, with healthcare and consumer-staples shares leading gains.

See also: Asian stocks rise on signal Fed may not need aggressive rate hikes

The pressure on chip stocks eased after Nvidia Corp chief executive officer Jensen Huang defended the financial health of AI computing supplier CoreWeave Inc. The company’s shares rose 4%, after a 12% tumble in the previous session. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index pared its losses to less than 1%, having earlier fallen as much as 4.4%.

“CoreWeave’s strength is improving every day,” Huang told Bloomberg at an event on Thursday in Stockholm. “I am optimistic. Their cost of capital is actually decreasing.”

In other corners of the market, the dollar weakened, while gold climbed in the last session. US crude oil edged lower on Friday to about US$97.50 a barrel.

Meanwhile, questions over the durability of the AI investment boom are spilling into credit markets as investors scrutinise the debt financing the infrastructure buildout.

A measure of CoreWeave’s credit risk climbed to an all-time high on Thursday as some of its high-yield bonds extended declines.

On Warsh, traders will look for clues on whether Fed officials are leaning towards another rate increase. Last month, Fed officials lifted borrowing costs for the first time since 2023 and futures now imply about a 25% chance of a rate hike in October.

“On balance, we think Warsh will talk in a way that does not suggest an October hike,” said Krishna Guha at Evercore. “Warsh will be mindful of the global wobble in tech stocks and signs financing conditions are tightening for more exposed AI names, on top of the prior move up in longer-term yields.”

title: MSCI weighs downgrade of Indonesia to remove from global indexes
article:
(Oct 16) : Indonesia faces a potential ejection from global stock indexes after MSCI Inc. said the country no longer merits emerging-market status, escalating the threat of foreign investor flight as concerns deepen over market integrity.

The index provider is consulting on a proposal to reclassify Indonesia as a standalone market, saying a downgrade to frontier status would not adequately reflect the severity of the country’s market problems. MSCI expects to proceed with the change unless it finds clear evidence of material improvements in market governance and functioning.

Despite reforms announced by Indonesian authorities, “significant concerns remain around market dysfunction, including continued suspected coordinated trading behaviour

and lack of evidence of meaningful enforcement,” MSCI said in a statement Thursday.

Standalone status is reserved for markets that don’t meet MSCI’s criteria for inclusion in either its emerging- or frontier-market indexes. Argentina, Lebanon and Palestine are among the markets with the designation, with none in Asia. For Southeast Asia’s largest economy, the proposed reclassification would mark a major setback in its efforts to attract global investment.

The move threatens to deepen pressure on a market already reeling from concerns over its investability. MSCI warned in January of a potential downgrade to frontier status, triggering a historic rout. Indonesia’s benchmark stock index has fallen about 32% in 2026, making it the worst performer among global peers.

See also: Asian stocks set for gains as tech selloff eases

A standalone classification could force passive funds tracking MSCI’s emerging-market indexes to sell Indonesian holdings, while active managers benchmarked against those indexes may also cut exposure. Losing access to both emerging- and frontier-market benchmarks could further weaken foreign investor demand, putting additional pressure on share prices and liquidity.

The consultation will run through April 30, 2027, with a final decision expected by June 30, MSCI said.

Indonesian authorities have announced a series of reforms aimed at averting a downgrade, including enhanced disclosure of shareholders with ownership above 1%, more detailed investor classifications and a roadmap toward a minimum free-float requirement of 15%. But MSCI has said investors need to see consistent implementation and evidence that the measures are materially improving market functioning. MSCI in June postponed its review on the nation’s equities, saying it needs more time to see whether recently announced transparency measures are effective.

See also: Stock buyers step in to power Wall Street rebound

In the Thursday announcement, MSCI said it will also maintain its freeze on certain index changes involving Indonesian securities until further notice.

title: Stock buyers step in to power Wall Street rebound
article:
(Oct 16) : Wall Street staged a comeback after losses driven by concerns about the sustainability of the artificial-intelligence trade that has powered the bull market in stocks.

The S&P 500 halted a three-day drop. A selloff in chipmakers eased as Nvidia Corp.’s chief Jensen Huang defended the financial health of AI computing supplier CoreWeave Inc., a major customer in which the company is also an investor. That was after a measure of credit risk at the data-center operator hit an all-time high, triggering fresh jitters about the AI sector.

In a sign of rotation to other sectors, an equal-weighted version of the S&P 500 — which strips out market-value biases — climbed 1.4%. Worries about the durability of the AI investment cycle have also intensified a debate about whether bonds are offering value after a plunge that had sent yields to multi-year highs.

Concerns about CoreWeave’s viability have contributed to a recent rout in stocks amid speculation that the massive buildout of AI infrastructure has outrun the ability of companies to get a return on their investments.

Given the extraordinary amounts of debt being taken on to build out AI infrastructure, higher borrowing costs are far from ideal, according to David Morrison at Trade Nation.

“Two questions matter. Is demand for AI real? Yes,” said Manish Singh at Crossbridge Capital. “Are we going back to working and using software as we did before AI? No. The structural opportunity is real, but that does not mean every company building the infrastructure will generate attractive returns for investors.”

See also: Asian stocks to fall after US chipmaker sellof

Ultimately, the AI revolution will be judged not just by how much computing power we build, but by how profitably we use it, Singh noted. Future cash flows must justify today’s enormous capital commitments, and someone must finance the gap in the meantime, he said.

“AI may be the future. Debt servicing is still the present,” Singh concluded.

Looking ahead, all eyes will be on Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh’s remarks for clues on whether officials are pivoting from a skip to an October rate-hike in light of the latest inflation data, according to Krishna Guha at Evercore.

See also: Oil holds advance as expanding Middle East war threatens supply

“On balance, we think Warsh will talk in a way that does not suggest an October hike,” Guha said. “Warsh will be mindful of the global wobble in tech stocks and signs financing conditions are tightening for more exposed AI names, on top of the prior move up in longer-term yields.”

The Fed chief is due to speak late Thursday New York time in Bangkok, where he is scheduled to appear in a fireside chat with International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva.
